Before we start

What your business needs in place.

None of this is code, and all of it can stall a launch for weeks if it surfaces late. Shipping on my developer account removes the first three outright.

A legal identity for the accountnot needed on my account

Google Play accepts an individual. Apple accepts an individual too, but then the app publishes under your personal name rather than a brand. A company account needs the commercial registration or equivalent documents.

12 testers, if the Play account is brand newnot needed on my account

Google requires personal developer accounts opened after November 2023 to run a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days before it will even consider production access — and since 2026 it checks the testers actually used the app. That is roughly three weeks before a first launch, and it is the single biggest thing standing between a new account and a live listing.

A D-U-N-S number, for an Apple company accountnot needed on my account

Apple will not enrol an organisation without one. It is free and Apple arranges it, but it can take up to two weeks — this is the single most common reason a launch date slips.

The right to the app name and the brand

Both stores reject a listing that impersonates someone else, and a trademark complaint takes a live app down later rather than at review. If the name is already taken on the store, we find that out before writing the listing, not after.

A privacy policy that matches what the app actually does

Both stores require a public URL, and Apple compares it against the data the app collects. A copied template that claims you collect nothing while the app has analytics is a rejection. I write and host one if you do not have it.

A support channel somebody answers

An email address at minimum. Apple checks it during review, and it is where your users go when something breaks.

Tax and banking details — only if the app takes money

Paid apps, subscriptions and in-app purchases need the store's tax forms and a payout bank account before the app can charge anyone. A free app skips this entirely.

A decision on whose account it lives under

This is the one that changes both the price and the paperwork. If you want to be live this week and the company documents are not ready, shipping on my account is the answer.

Marked items are not needed at all when the app ships on my developer account.

Assets and images

What the stores want, at the size they want it.

Each one drawn at the shape the store asks for. Send what you have; the rest I can make.

App icon

Apple App Store and Google Play

1024 × 1024PNG · no transparency, no rounded corners

Apple wants a square 1024 with square corners — the store rounds them itself. Play takes 512, which I resize from the same master, so one file covers both.

required

Feature graphic

Google Play

1024 × 500PNG or JPG · no transparency

The banner across the top of a Play listing. Play will not publish without it. Keep text away from the edges — it gets cropped on some surfaces.

required

Phone screenshots

Apple App Store and Google Play

1290 × 2796 · 9:19.5PNG or JPG · 2 to 8 per store

The only thing most people look at. Apple asks for the largest iPhone size and scales the rest down; Play accepts any tall ratio between 320 and 3840 px a side.

required

Tablet screenshots

Apple App Store and Google Play

2064 × 2752 · 3:4PNG or JPG · 2 to 8

Required by Apple the moment the app supports iPad, and by Play for tablet-targeted listings. Skipping it on a tablet-capable app is a rejection, not a warning.

if the app runs on tablets

Preview video

Apple App Store and Google Play

16:9 or the screenshot sizePlay: a YouTube link · Apple: 15–30s

Lifts installs when it shows the app being used in the first three seconds. Worth skipping entirely rather than shipping a slideshow.

optional

Exact device sizes shift when Apple and Google ship new hardware, so I confirm the current list against the console the week we submit. What does not change: one 1024 icon master and a set of tall phone screenshots covers most of it.

How it runs

Six steps, and you see each one.

  1. 01

    Handover

    You send the build, the copy and the artwork. Within a day you get a written list of anything missing.

  2. 02

    Accounts and signing

    Accounts opened, keystore and certificates generated or imported, bundle IDs reserved — documented and handed to you. Done carelessly, this is the step that breaks every future update.

  3. 03

    Listing built

    Listing written AR/EN, screenshots sized per store, privacy and data-safety declarations completed.

  4. 04

    Test track

    An internal Play track and a TestFlight build first. You approve it on a real device before anyone else sees it.

  5. 05

    Submission and review

    Submitted to both. Listing comments answered the same day, no cap on rounds; build comments come back to you with the exact fix.

  6. 06

    Live, then handover

    Rollout, then credentials, keystore, certificates and a short doc on shipping the next version. The 30 days start here.

Right fit, wrong fit

Saves a call that would end in no.

A good fit

  • The app is finished and runs on a real device
  • You would rather not learn two developer consoles for one launch
  • You need Arabic and English on the listing, done properly
  • You have no company yet, or Apple's verification would take longer than your deadline
  • You want one person answerable through both reviews

Not a fit

  • The app is not built yet, or half-built
  • It needs a feature added before a store would accept it
  • You want installs and reviews rather than a listing — that is marketing, not publishing
  • You want the cheapest possible number and nothing else matters

After launch

Support, once it is live.

Stores change policy, deadlines land without warning, and one rejection can pull a live app down. Every package includes 30 days after launch; the Care plan keeps someone on the hook after that.

Questions

The ones people actually ask.

I do not have a company. Can I still publish?

Yes. Google Play accepts an individual account. Apple accepts an individual developer account too, though it publishes under your personal name rather than a brand. If you want a brand name without a company, the cleanest route is shipping on my developer account.

What happens if the app is rejected?

I answer it. Rejections are normal — missing test credentials, an unclear privacy declaration, a permission with no stated purpose. Handling them is part of the package, not an extra round. There is no cap on resubmissions.

Do you write the app as well?

This service is publishing only — it assumes a build that already works. If the app still needs building or fixing, that is a separate scope and I will quote it separately rather than fold it in here.

If it ships on your account, who owns the app?

You do. You keep the code, the assets and the store content, and the listing carries your brand. The developer account is the only thing that is mine, and the app can be transferred to your own account whenever you want it — I handle the transfer at cost.

How long does it actually take?

Three to seven days on accounts that can already publish — Google usually reviews in a day or two, Apple is stricter and slower but normally inside 48 hours. A brand-new personal Play account is a different story: Google makes you run a 14-day closed test with 12 real testers before it will grant production access, so a first launch there is closer to three weeks. A new Apple company account adds the D-U-N-S wait on top. Shipping on my account skips both, because my accounts already publish. On top of any of that, budget a day or two for each round of review comments — most first submissions get at least one — and a week of slack overall if the launch date matters to someone.

Can you publish an app that was already live and got taken down?

Usually. Tell me the reason given in the notice before we start — a policy strike on an account is a different problem from a rejected build, and it changes which route makes sense.

Tell me what you have, and I will tell you what it takes.

The app, the market and the deadline is enough to get a straight answer on scope, price and timing — usually the same day.
